task: Write one sentence of your own using the word aggrieved. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know aggrieved should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Aggrieved season-ticket holders demanded refunds when the club moved its biggest home game to a stadium four hundred miles away.
Miffed is much milder than aggrieved — a miffed guest is briefly annoyed at some small slight and forgets it by dessert.
Embittered goes further than aggrieved — the sense of being wronged has hardened over years into permanent bitterness.

Wronged states the plain fact that an injustice was done to you — cheated, robbed, betrayed. Aggrieved names what that fact leaves behind: the wounded, brooding sense of unfair treatment a person carries afterward. You are wronged the day it happens; you stay aggrieved long after.

Offended means your dignity has been hurt by an insult or a slight, with no real injury required. Aggrieved is heavier: it claims a genuine wrong was actually done to you. A snub at the door leaves you offended; a stolen patent leaves you aggrieved.

The union rep keeps every grievance from the past decade in a blue binder on her desk.
Aggrieved means distressed, wronged, injured.
The inventor left the awards banquet aggrieved: the machine on the stage was her design, patented under her employer's name while she was told the project had been scrapped.
She did not shout; she hired a lawyer.
Aggrieved is more precise than 'upset' or 'angry' because it always contains a claim of injustice — someone did you wrong, and the hurt comes wrapped around that fact.
Courts still call the injured party 'the aggrieved.'

Aggrieved is the word for someone nursing a justified sense of injustice — contracts and courtrooms even speak of 'the aggrieved party.' Plain 'upset' or 'annoyed' misses the claim of unfairness at its core.
And unlike its unit-mate anguish, which is crushing inner sorrow, aggrieved points outward, at the wrong that was done to you.
